options.content:
# Profiler Pipeline Health

**Is JFR profiling actually working?** Eighteen `edl_jfr_*` families are collected and
nothing read them until this page, so a profiler that had silently stopped attaching,
or was shipping nothing, looked exactly like a healthy one.

Read the top row first. It answers, in order: do we want to profile this node, did we
manage to attach to the JVM, and did the last recording reach the server. Everything
below the top row explains a red light in it.

**Two counters that look alike and are not.** Pruning **for age** is routine
housekeeping. Pruning **unshipped** chunks is data loss: a recording was deleted before
it ever left the node. Pruning **for size** sits between the two and means the local
budget is too small for the recording rate.

**`edl_jfr_ship_last_success_timestamp_seconds` is 0 on a node that has never shipped.**
`time() - 0` is the whole Unix epoch, so every staleness panel filters with `> 0` and a
node that has never shipped is absent rather than wrong by fifty years. Check the
desired-versus-attached panel to tell "never shipped" from "not profiled".

The only label on these families is `host_name`, so **Group by** offers nothing else
useful; each panel names the dimension it honours.

panels.title: Nodes profiling desired
panels.description: How many selected nodes are configured to be profiled. Zero here means the profiler is off by configuration, not broken.

panels.title: Nodes attached
panels.description: How many selected nodes currently hold a live JFR session on the target JVM.

panels.title: Desired but NOT attached
panels.description: The gap between intent and reality. Anything above zero means at least one node is meant to be profiled and is not. This is the single most important number on the page.

panels.title: Nodes with unreadable config
panels.description: edl_jfr_config_unreadable. The reconciler could not read its own profiling config on these nodes, so it cannot know what is wanted. Expected to be set on nodes that are not database nodes and were never given a config.

panels.title: Time since last successful ship (worst node)
panels.description: The best single staleness signal on the page. Computed as time() - edl_jfr_ship_last_success_timestamp_seconds, filtered with > 0 so nodes that never shipped do not report the age of the Unix epoch. Green under 5 minutes, amber under 15, red beyond.

panels.title: Chunks pending (worst node)
panels.description: Recordings written locally and not yet shipped. A steady small number is normal; a number that only grows means shipping is slower than recording.

panels.title: JFR bytes on disk (all selected nodes)
panels.description: Local spool size across the selected nodes. Read it beside the prune-for-size counter: growth that stops abruptly usually means the size cap started deleting recordings.

panels.title: Unshipped chunks pruned in this window
panels.description: DATA LOSS. Recordings deleted before they were ever shipped. Any value above zero means profiles that were captured no longer exist anywhere. Window follows the dashboard time range.

panels.title: Attach failures in this window
panels.description: edl_jfr_attach_failures_total. The reconciler tried to attach and the attach raised an error. Window follows the dashboard time range.

panels.title: Attach skips in this window
panels.description: edl_jfr_attach_skipped_total. The reconciler declined to attach, for example because no target JVM was running yet. Skips are not errors, but a node that only ever skips is never profiled.

panels.title: Ship failures in this window
panels.description: edl_jfr_ship_failures_total. The upload was attempted and failed. Retried, so a few are survivable; a rising count with rising chunks pending is not.

panels.title: Ship rejections in this window
panels.description: edl_jfr_ship_rejected_total. The server received the recording and refused it. Unlike a failure this will not succeed on retry, so the recording is lost unless something changes on the receiving side.

panels.title: Attach — are we profiling what we meant to?
Profiling Desired vs Session Attached, per Node
panels.description: Two gauges that should sit on top of each other. Where the desired line is above the attached line, that node is meant to be profiled and is not. Honoured dimension: host_name.

panels.title: Attach Outcomes per Second by $groupby
panels.description: Failures, skips, deferrals and successful session starts as rates. A node that restarts its session constantly loses the continuity that makes a profile comparable across a run.

panels.title: Shipping — did the recordings leave the node?
Time Since Last Successful Ship, per Node (s)
panels.description: A sawtooth is healthy: it climbs between ships and drops to zero on each success. A line that only climbs is a node that has stopped shipping. Nodes that have never shipped are filtered out by > 0 and are simply absent.

panels.title: Ship Outcomes per Second by $groupby
panels.description: Failures retry; rejections do not. Separating them matters because only one of the two resolves on its own.

panels.title: Chunks Pending per Node
panels.description: The shipping backlog. Flat near zero is healthy. A ramp means the node is producing recordings faster than it can upload them, and the prune counters below will start moving next.

panels.title: JFR Bytes on Disk per Node
panels.description: Local spool size. Compare its shape with the chunks-pending panel: bytes rising while chunks stay flat means the recordings themselves are getting bigger, which is a profiler-settings question, not a shipping one.

panels.title: Prune Rate by Reason (chunks/s)
panels.description: Three different meanings, deliberately not summed. FOR AGE is routine retention. FOR SIZE means the local budget is smaller than the recording rate. UNSHIPPED is data loss: the recording was deleted before it ever left the node. Only the last one is an incident.

panels.title: Current State Flags per Node
panels.description: The gauge-valued flags, plotted so a transition is visible in time rather than only as a number. Attach deferred means the reconciler is waiting for something before it attaches; ship truncated means the last upload was cut short; config unreadable means it does not know what is wanted.

list.description: Every node the profiling reconciler reports on, not only database nodes: a control or application node with an unreadable config is a real finding. All expands to the explicit list; allValue is deliberately unset.
list.label: Host
list.name: host

list.description: The edl_jfr_* families carry only host_name and cluster, so those are the only meaningful choices. Panels that plot per-node gauges ignore this variable and always break out by host_name.
list.label: Group by
list.name: groupby
